text.p: Singapore's stock market is beginning to benefit from its reputation as a slightly dull but extremely safe place to put money, fund managers say.

Falls on the Tokyo stock market and signs that Hong Kong's bourse may have peaked appear to be encouraging many institutional investors to reassess Singapore, which has badly underperformed rival bourses over the last three years.
"Singapore has a 'safe haven' status," said Hugh Young, director of Abtrust Fund Managers in Singapore.
"With Tokyo falling, Hong Kong having gone up a hell of a lot, and few people wanting to go into Thailand, Singapore is becoming more of an option."
Regional analysts say most funds are re-weighting Singapore, partly at the expense of Hong Kong.

No matter how small the risk of turbulence associated with the handover of power in Hong Kong to China from Britain on July 1, the territory's stock market has risen dramatically over the last year, and analysts think the rally cannot last much longer.
That automatically frees up several extra percentage points of weighting to divert to other Asian markets outside Japan.

In addition, big falls in Japan's Nikkei in the last few weeks have pushed a number of flexible institutions, including some pension and mutual funds, out of Tokyo and in search of other relatively risk-free investments in Asia.

Most Southeast Asian bourses appear to be benefiting slightly from this outflow and many funds say they are spreading investments through emerging markets, including Manila, Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta and Bangkok.
But within Southeast Asia, Singapore appears to be attracting a higher proportion of new funds than in recent times.
"The feeling we've had from funds is that they are looking to push up their weighting in Singapore," said Neil Payne, head of equity research at ING Baring in Singapore.

"Singapore has been sold down to around eight or nine percent of Asia ex-Japan funds over the last year -- a significant under-weighting," he said. "But now that is moving back to around 12 percent or higher, which is a more neutral position."
Singapore stocks have underperformed since 1994.
The benchmark Straits Times Index closed on Friday at 2,242.71 points, around eight percent below its level a year ago and little changed from its position in January 1994.

While average Singapore share values have risen several percentage points a year in U.S. dollar terms as the Singapore dollar has appreciated, analysts point out that corporate earnings growth has still far outstripped these gains.
And Singapore has a number of other attractions.

Politically and economically untra-stable, and based in a very strong currency, most of its blue chip companies have conservative management that takes few risks. This denies them some of the spectacular growth seen in other emerging markets.
But they are safe, well primed with capital-intensive high technology and still gaining from the region's booming demand.
The Singapore economy also appears about to emerge from a year-long slowdown in manufacturing growth and exports that was triggered by the global slump in demand for electronics.

"There is a recognition that the trough of the slowdown has been passed," said Mano Sabnani, head of research at DBS Securities in Singapore. "That seems to be a good trigger for foreign investors to move in."
